methodological_rigor.justification: The MELODY trial is a two-arm randomized noninferiority comparative-effectiveness study at two US cancer centers with n=300, previously published protocol (ref 43), full allocation concealment, randomization stratified by site, anxiety medication, and language, and masking of the PI and biostatistician. Intention-to-treat analysis with linear mixed-effects models for repeated measures, prespecified noninferiority margins (0.35 SD; actual margins 1.20 and 1.28), treatment fidelity checklists (80% item threshold with retraining), and Benjamini-Hochberg correction for heterogeneity tests are all rigorous. Limitations include absence of a usual-care/placebo arm (acknowledged), highly educated predominantly female sample (breast cancer ~50%), and self-reported generalized anxiety disorder status.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Anxiety affects ~50% of cancer survivors and CBT access is limited. Demonstrating that telehealth music therapy is noninferior to first-line CBT at both 8 and 26 weeks, with ~70% MCID response rates in both arms, directly expands evidence-based options and supports integrative oncology guidelines (ASCO-SIO). The telehealth format, Spanish-language inclusion, and use of board-certified music therapists enhance real-world clinical applicability. Oxford LoE 1b as an individual RCT.

reporting_quality.justification: CONSORT diagram is presented, coprimary endpoints with noninferiority margins are prespecified, treatment fidelity (91-97% of sessions) is documented, heterogeneity analyses are prespecified with FDR control, and adverse events, adherence, and sensitivity analyses for generalized anxiety disorder are reported. Trial protocol was previously published. Explicit CONSORT checklist reference is not visible, and while REDCap and R version are cited, no specific data-sharing statement beyond the supplementary protocol is apparent.

novelty_literature.justification: While both interventions exist in oncology and telehealth CBT has been extensively studied, this is the first randomized head-to-head noninferiority trial of music therapy vs CBT for anxiety in cancer survivors with long-term (26-week) follow-up. Prior Cochrane meta-analyses had only evaluated short-term effects. The demonstration of durable equivalence with a scalable active-music-therapy protocol (collaborative songwriting) constitutes a meaningful novel contribution that could inform guideline updates.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized with clear prespecified hypotheses, treatment protocol descriptions grounded in theoretical frameworks (social-cognitive processing model, cognitive-behavioral model), and transparent reporting of limitations. Figures 1-2 and Tables 1-2 communicate key results effectively. The discussion thoughtfully interprets findings including heterogeneity of treatment effects by education and years since diagnosis.

key_strengths: First randomized noninferiority head-to-head trial of telehealth music therapy vs CBT for anxiety in cancer survivors with 26-week follow-up
Appropriately prespecified noninferiority margins (0.35 SD) and coprimary endpoints at weeks 8 and 26
Both arms achieved MCID-exceeding improvements with ~70% response rates and durable effects
Rigorous fidelity monitoring (91-97%) across 14 interventionists with clear retraining protocols
Inclusion of Spanish-speaking and diverse patients enhances generalizability and real-world relevance
key_concerns: No usual-care or attention control arm, limiting ability to separate specific from nonspecific treatment effects
Sample is mostly female, highly educated, with ~50% breast cancer; limits generalizability
Generalized anxiety disorder status based on self-report rather than clinician assessment
Slight adherence/attrition imbalance favoring music therapy (91.2% vs 82.4% completing 6 sessions)
Heterogeneity findings (CBT less effective with more years since diagnosis; education effect) should be confirmed
chief_reviewer.rationale: A well-designed noninferiority RCT with direct implications for integrative oncology practice; appropriate for a high-impact tier-1 oncology journal with minor revisions.
